utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Examination-in-chief is still continuing. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Weiner [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. Are you feeling better today?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm feeling very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If at any time you don't feel well, would you please just notify the Judges or the Court, if you're not feeling well.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we left off on Thursday, we were discussing situations where local residents were giving bribes to the defendant Miroslav Tadic and Sveto Vasovic in order to get out of Bosanski Samac. Do you recall that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that a number of people told you after they left how they bribed these two persons.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us about Juro Krajinovic who was a director at the Mladost company?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us how he paid some 5.000 Deutschmarks to the defendant Miroslav Tadic to get his family out of Bosanski Samac in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was the first family to leave Samac, the first Croatian family, that is, as far as I know. Maybe there were some who left even earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were they exchanged as part of the exchange programme or were they just driven out pursuant to the bribe, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miro Brko drove them out in his own car. It was not an exchange. It was a private service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say Miro Brko, are you referring to the defendant Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I apologise. Miroslav Tadic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing to apologise for. As you keep on referring to him as Miroslav Brko, is that because in Tadic -- I'm sorry - in Samac don't everyone -- doesn't everyone have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If somebody were asking for me by my full name, nobody would know who they were looking for. We use only nicknames, and that's how we know each other, by nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue on with the bribes to be released from Bosanski Samac. Did any members of your family - nieces, nephews, any of your relatives - bribe -- use a bribe to get out of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When my brother's son, Abdulah Avdo Drljacic was exchanged or rather when he was supposed to be exchanged and was brought for that purpose from Batkovic, his mother, wife, and children were supposed to accompany him. However, his mother was eventually allowed to come, but not his wife, under the pretext that she was under her work obligation. She was a very beautiful woman, I must say. They got around to gathering all their jewellery in a small box, and Avdo's wife went to Sveto and told him, "Uncle Sveto, you forgot this box." He didn't look what was inside, but he supposed it was a bribe, and she was eventually allowed to go to the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, her name was -- what was her name, your niece who bribed Sveto? What was her name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drljacic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was her first name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadila Drljacic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she handed Sveto Vasovic this box filled with jewellery?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever they had, they gave him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't return the box, did he?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He knew it was meant for him. He knew very well that he hadn't forgotten anything. It was just a trick. But they understood each other very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did she know to go to Sveto with a bribe?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sveto was the one who read out the names of people who were allowed to go on the bus for exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic. Can you start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. The question is formulated in such a way as to ask the witness to speculate as to what another person was thinking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just trying to get some information basically what was the knowledge of her niece, if she knows, how did she know to go to Sveto. And I was going to ask the follow-up question: Was it basically a public secret if you want to call it, that everyone knew who to bribe in Bosanski Samac to get out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can ask, adding the latter part of your explanation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, ma'am. Rather than look at your daughter's thoughts - I'm sorry, your niece's thoughts - was it public knowledge in Bosanski Samac who you had to bribe to get on the exchange list or to get out of the Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't know. If I had known about it then, I would have tried the same thing. However, only after I was exchanged other people told me, "How come you didn't know that you could go to Sveto or Miro and pay them? You could have left earlier."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after your daughter gave the bribe to Sveto, was she exchanged?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is not my daughter; she is the daughter-in-law of my brother. She was allowed to go to -- to board that bus after she handed him that box, that jewellery box.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your niece Fadila, Fadila. So she was allowed to be exchanged after she made the bribe?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She immediately boarded the bus, which left for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us move on to your exchange. Let's move on to December 24th, 1993. Now, prior to your being exchanged, within a week prior to your being exchanged, did you go to see someone to request to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happened.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My next-door neighbour, named Maslic, I think his first name was Vjekoslav Maslic, in any case, he was a minister at the Red Cross. And I went to see him without any idea about whether there was supposed to be an exchange. I went there just to talk to him, because I couldn't find him at his apartment for a while before that. So when I came to him, I said, "I'm sorry. I didn't come to see you as a neighbour or as a minister. I came to talk to you as a human being, considering that you know that my daughter is living in Croatia and is married to a Serb, could I possibly, in case I am exchanged, create for them even greater difficulties than they are already experiencing?" And he answered, "You have to go."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just take a step back. Why did you feel you would create greater difficulties by going to -- by getting exchange and meeting them or living with them?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the situation in which we Muslims were in, we were totally disenfranchised. I didn't know whether they were in the same position in Croatia. And at the time there was a conflict between Muslims and Croats, a serious conflict, and my daughter was a Muslim and her husband was a Serb. I didn't know what situation they were in. And he, regardless of the side he was on, should know more than I about the situation over there. So that's why I went to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he said to you, "You have to go"?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long after he said, "You have to go" were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely at the time when they were supposed to clear out the camp in Zasavica. Of course I didn't know anything about that. But that coincided, luckily for me, with the time of my conversation. It was a day or to before that. A courier, Muslim, who was under work obligation delivering messages, came to my home and said, "Tomorrow you and Piko should be ready to go to the venue of an exchange." I was very surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me just get this straight. You meet with Maslic, and then a few days --

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the municipality in the Red Cross office, and there was a sign on his door saying: Minister and his name, Vladimiro or Vjekoslav Maslic. I don't know his first name precisely. I've mentioned it before, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many days later did the courier come to your house after you met with Maslic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two after my discussion with Maslic, maybe even the following day, but it was late in the evening, or night, when he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did they tell you to report at a certain location?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were to be outside the local commune at 7.30 in the morning, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," you mean you and Piko. Who was Piko?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Piko is my brother, Teufik Drljacic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you reported, I believe, on December 24th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, at half past 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got there, did you see any of the defendants at the local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we underwent a search. They asked us what we were carrying. I had a travel bag. And I said it was a travel bag containing things that belonged to me and my brother. Nobody searched any of my things. I just boarded the bus. I don't know whether the others were searched. It was not an exchange, but it was labelled as an exchange. We were accompanied by Miroslav Tadic and this Maslic, plus some policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see the defendant Miroslav Tadic at the local commune on that morning when you gathered?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was outside the local commune, but in any case, we saw him in Gradiska. That was where we crossed the Sava River and that's where we saw each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone call out the names for those to board the bus?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all those who were on the list - and I really can't remember any more whether the list was read out outside the bus. It probably was, lest somebody who wasn't on the list got on the bus. I can't remember such details, because I wasn't very composed. You can't be very composed at such moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you got on the bus. Did your brother Piko enter the bus too?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was together with me on the bus. However, it was the time when they were clearing out the camp in Zasavica, and there was a separate bus for the people who had been in that camp, Muslims, plus a few Croats who had been left over, the former owners of those homes. So they picked up the leftover Croats, the original inhabitants of the village, plus the Muslims who had been sent to camp there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's stay at the local commune first before we get to Zasavica. Were many people on the bus at the local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was packed to such an extent that we barely had standing room. We sat on our things, on our luggage. People sat in each other's lap. Mr. Miroslav Tadic is perhaps better placed to describe it than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Tadic accompanied the bus. Did he get on the bus or did he go in a separate vehicle?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he travelled in a separate vehicle, although we saw him in Gradiska. But after we crossed the Sava River and got on the Croatian side, we drove for a while, back and forth, back and forth, for a long time, and we didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just stop. We've got to get to Zasavica first before we get to Croatia. Let's take it one step at a time. On the bus, were there men, women, were there soldiers? Who were these people placed on the bus with you and your brother? Were these children? As best you can recall.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Women, children, and elderly men. For instance, there was one Ago Hadziabdic, Reuf's father born in 1913 who had previously been in Batkovici, and I don't know where he had been detained before Batkovici. And after he was brought from Batkovici, he was transported to Zasavica again, and he got out at the same time as I did. It was the last exchange, although it wasn't really an exchange. I don't know what it was. You can decide that for yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This 80-year-old man who was being held in Batkovici and Zasavica, of what ethnic group did he belong?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. It's Reuf Hadziabdic's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his physical condition, if you can recall? Was he a well man? Was he sickly?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very ill even before that, and especially so after all the torture he had gone through. He wasn't able even to walk properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the local commune, you go to Zasavica. Can you describe the people who got on the bus at Zasavica? Are we talking about women, children, soldiers? Who was placed on that bus at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our bus didn't enter Zasavica. They were loaded on buses there. But I know a couple of people who were put on buses in Zasavica. For instance, my cousin, Fatima; then a disabled woman, Fatima Barjaktarevic. These women had been driven out of their homes to make room for Serbs who wanted to move in. And that was my case too. I was driven out of my apartment so that somebody else could move in, although I never found out who exactly moved in after I was expelled. For the most part, those were civilians: Women, children, and a few men, elderly men, including that old man born in 1913.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them loading these people or placing these people on the bus at Zasavica or did you arrive there and already see a bus of people waiting out front?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their bus drove either in front of ours or behind ours, but we met up in Vrhpolje. And when we got off in Dragalici, we saw them. In any case, they were separate from us. And I was like lost. I didn't know what to expect. I thought we would intermingle and swap places. And this Maslic, my neighbour, told me at one point, "Why don't you go and join all the others?" I don't know how I got to the bus and how I got on that bus. I don't know whether it was an exchange or a mopping up operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have a question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, a little bit of a clarification question here. I'm a little bit unclear, the talk of people from Zasavica getting on buses and so on. It appeared, Mr. Weiner, for some of your questions that you were under the impression that the witness had been in Zasavica herself. I'd just like a clarification re: The witness enters the bus in Bosanski Samac. Is it true that people were brought from Zasavica to the retirement municipal building and also boarded a different, separate bus there, and then they went to the exchange point? I'd just like to get the scenario a little bit clearer than I have it in my mind at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to develop that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The Judge has some questions, ma'am. The persons on the bus from Zasavica, you indicated there were two buses. You got on one. Did persons from Zasavica enter the bus that you were on? Just that question first. Did persons from Zasavica enter your bus?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had a separate bus. Their bus was separate. They entered the bus in Zasavica. Zasavica is six kilometres away -- further away from Samac. We were all civilians, but those civilians that were not in the camp were in one bus, and those that were in the camp were in the other bus, so that we had no contact with each other. I'd also like to add the following. I apologise for being late. When we crossed onto the Croatian side and when we were supposed to exit the bus, and this time while we were being driven back and forth, we had no idea what was going on. At that moment, Miroslav Tadic entered the bus that I was on and said the following: "The Croatians won't take you. You have nowhere to return to because gubars are in your houses."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's once again take a one step at a time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, could we find out what gubars means too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll do that one first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe -- could you define the word "gubar"?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain it as well as I can. Basically, those are insects that destroy trees. It's some kind of a caterpillar, so some kind of a pest, but I'm not quite sure what he meant when he said this to us. I think he would be the one to explain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At some point you stop after driving around; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, she is having trouble with her earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point -- let's take it slowly, one step at a time. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At some point you stop. You have two buses: One from Zasavica and one from Bosanski Samac, and at some point you stop and Miroslav Tadic enters the bus. Where are you at that point?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the bus that Tadic entered. This was in the evening. They couldn't stay with us. It seemed that this would take a long time. So he said, "We are going to sleep in Gradiska. Croats won't take you in, and you have nowhere to go, because these pests, these insects, are already in your homes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were removed from your homes, people of what ethnic group moved into your homes?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs were moving in, but I don't know the specific person, the particular person that moved into my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't go back to Bosanski Samac at that time because people were moving into your homes; is that correct, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But we also didn't want to return home. We were very happy to be leaving. We were -- we expected to leave for freedom, because we had no freedom where we had been before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happens -- you're at a point, you've been sitting there, told you're going to stay for the evening, that the Croats don't want you. Do you get exchanged that day?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Mr. Miroslav and Mr. Maslic left, a police officer got on the bus and he asked us to collect 200 Deutschmarks for them, since they had to stay with us. We collected as much as we could. It could also be the case that some of us couldn't show everything we had, so there was some difficulty, but at the end we managed to collect 200 Deutschmarks and they left us alone. What they did after that, I don't know. We were on the bus without any policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you eventually exchanged, or were you eventually given the right to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This all happened in the evening, and this was just before the Catholic Christmas. This exchange or this cleansing wasn't reported to the Croatians, because they were at midnight mass, I assumed. After the midnight mass was over - I don't know exactly when, sometime after midnight - we were told that the Croatian buses arrived and we were allowed to leave our buses. We disembarked our buses. It was raining very heavily. And I already mentioned to you that I was very lost, that I didn't know which way to turn. I waited for some kind of a line to form. But I already said this to you before, so I don't want to repeat myself. But all this happened after midnight on the 25th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see Miroslav Tadic there while you were sent over to the Croatian buses?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Miroslav personally, but I believe he was there. I saw Maslic, however, and Maslic was telling me where to go. I was completely lost. At some point I had remained entirely by myself and he was directing me. But Miroslav must have been there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said at that point you wanted to leave for freedom. Prior to then - let's go back to April, before the war started - in April, before the war started, did you want to leave Bosanski Samac, that town where your family had lived since the nineteenth century?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never wanted to leave my town, and I don't even want to leave it today. And even though I might not be welcome there, I want to return and die and be buried by my parents. However, the war in Croatia started before the Bosnian war, and my daughter lives in Croatia even today. They had to move from town to town because they were refugees. And as a mother, I was following my daughter, because my daughter had three young children, and she needed both physical and moral support. Therefore, I was in Croatia this whole time, but I would come to Samac to pay my bills and see the doctor, get my medication, because I've been sick for very many years. And so it happened that on the 15th of April, I came back to Samac, in the evening. I finished all my errands on Thursday, and then on Friday the Chetniks had arrived in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to April. Before the war, your brothers and sisters that were living in Samac, did any of them want to leave Samac prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, one of my brothers had lived in Zagreb for 20 or more years, so he did not live in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the ones who were living in Samac. Just the ones who were living in Samac. Did they want to leave?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never wanted to leave. They never even thought about it. We were born there and we thought we would be buried there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and the members of your family enjoy living in Samac at that time, prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. We had perfectly normal lives. And those people that later started calling us extremists, we were friends with them. I found it very strange that my neighbour talked to me up to the very last day of peace, and then when the Chetniks arrived, he all of a sudden didn't know me. We all lived together. My family is mixed, as I said. My daughter is married to a Serb, and he himself stems from a mixed marriage. He has no prejudices, he doesn't feel Serbian or Hungarian. He feels Croatian because he was born in Croatia as was his father and grandfather. They were all born in Croatia and he feels Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just take it one step. If not for the conditions that were placed on the Muslims and Croats, and the treatment of the non-Serb population, including the beatings and the jailings or the imprisonment, would you have left that area, you and the members of your family?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, and I will return to Samac, and that is where I want to rest my bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, have you recently got your apartment back in Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the apartment back after a lot of trouble. I was told that I should go to Mile Pancir --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to that -- we'll get to that shortly. Let's just take -- let's follow it. We'll do it orderly. When did you receive your apartment back? When did you get it back first?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it happened this year, in March or April that I got my keys back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically a few months ago?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, have you visited your apartment since you received it back?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the apartment. I had been there and I saw its condition. I had to find repairmen so that they could make it into a livable apartment again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what your apartment looked like when you got it back a few months ago.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apartment was in a new building and I lived in it for 13 or 14 years before the war, so this was a very new building. When I entered my apartment, however, you couldn't tell what colour the walls were, or anything else. Everything was very dirty, everything was ruined. I found the bigger pieces of my property. They hadn't been taken out, but they were so demolished that they had to be ruined except for one wardrobe, which might be salvaged yet, for example, if I changed the handles and so on and so forth. And maybe the kitchen could be refurbished. But everything else was so ruined that I had to remove it from the apartment. The wash machine worked, but it seemed so terrible to me that I said that I didn't want it. The neighbour that lived in the apartment below me said, "Please, don't throw it away. The machine still works, and I could use it, so why don't you give it to me." So I gave her my washing machine. And I told the men that they should carry out everything out of the apartment except for the wardrobe and the kitchen elements, and also a stove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any of the furniture that you had had in 1992, was any of that missing?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chairs were missing, and a wash basin in the bathroom, and also some tapestries were missing, some of the tapestries that were on the walls. I even found the lamps. They were broken, but my chandeliers were still there. So, as I said, other than the chairs, all my other furniture was still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your brothers and their families, did they lose anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all lost everything. The house belonging to two of my brothers -- the houses belonging to two of my brothers were destroyed, Abid's and Teufik's houses. They were destroyed because they were taking off the roof, the tiles, also the doors and the windows, and therefore rain was entering the house, and that's how it got ruined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took off the roofs and the doors from those homes?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is well known. The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you got your home back a few months ago. When did you first receive notice that you had the right to get your apartment back?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the notice from Geneva in 1998. I got this notice when I was in the States. And at the end of 1999 or early 2000, I went to Samac with this letter to Mile, and they laughed at me. They were wondering how come I got this letter from Geneva. So I couldn't accomplish anything. I went back to the States and I was only able to finish this business this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you got that notice from Geneva saying you could get your apartment back, you said you went to Mile. Who did you go to? Who was Mile?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He works there at the Ministry for Refugees and Displaced Persons. His name is Mile Pancir. I don't know his last name. I never knew it. But more than once he said the following: "Just say Mile Pancir sent you," because he would recommend to me who I should go and see if I wanted things done. I know Mile's mother very well. I've known her for many years. She worked in the production department of the same company where I worked at. His mother's name was Rada, but I never knew her last name either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise. Now, since I remembered Rada, I would like to say the following: Once when I was seeing off my dearest before they were supposed to be exchanged, and I showed you how I was walking, I couldn't -- after we -- after the exchange was done, we were all returning together, but I stayed behind. I was left behind because I couldn't walk. And then I heard Mile's mother Rada say the following. She was on a bike: "You motherfuckers, how many of you are still left? You should all be murdered." I didn't want to miss the opportunity to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's stick with Mile first. You went the first time in 1999 to see Mile Pancir. Where did you go? Did you see him in an office in Bosanski Samac or an office elsewhere? Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same office. I can't remember if it was Mile personally, because there was more than one person there. There are always more than one person there. I don't know if they work for him or what else they might be doing. But basically some of his co-workers. The first time they laughed at me when I came with this letter from Geneva. They laughed. Why would I get a letter from Geneva which would enable me to reclaim my apartment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to his office. Was that - just yes or no - was that in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the same office where I at the end got my apartment back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that. When -- when you went back to that office, did you see Mile Pancir, Mile, nicknamed Pancir, to get your home back, your apartment back?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first or the second time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second time. Not in 1999, but the Geneva letter. Did you eventually go back and see him concerning getting your apartment back?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happened.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came and I asked if I could get my apartment back, and Mile said, "How much will you give me so to make this -- to get this decision for you?" He knew I was coming from the States. And I said, "Well, I don't know how much you're asking for." He said, "Well, how about a hundred dollars?" I thought, once I got this decision, that everything would be okay. I agreed. I said, "Okay. I will give you the hundred dollars." Then he repeated, "So you will give me a hundred dollars for me to make you -- to get this decision for you, and then you will give me a further 500 dollars so I can clear out your apartment and also give you the keys back." I was very surprised, and for me that was a lot of money. Since I received social support in the States, I cannot make much money, and I only receive very little. So I receive this social help, and I am only entitled to this very minimal amount of money, and for me this was a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, can you control the witness, please? Let's get to what is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to finish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you give Mile Pancir this money? Did you give him these bribes?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first day when we were talking about this, I didn't even have a hundred dollars on me. I only had 60 dollars. I also gave him 50 Deutschmarks, and he said, "You're 15 dollars short." The second time when I came to get the decision and when he was supposed to tell me when the apartment would be emptied out, I agree with my son-in-law, to whom I told, "I will give him 500 Deutschmarks." And my son-in-law said, "Mother, don't cause trouble. We will give him 500 dollars." But I was very insistent and I gave him 500 Deutschmarks. Please let me finish. I gave him 500 Deutschmarks, he counted them and put them in the drawer, and he asked me, "What did you give me?" I said, "500." 500 what? 500 Deutschmarks. What did we agree on? Did we say 500 Deutschmarks or --? My son-in-law then interrupted and he said "Well, why don't you give me Deutschmarks back and I will give you dollars." My son-in-law gave 500 dollars and he took the 500 Deutschmarks from him. On the same day he told me the following, "You will give me 50 Deutschmarks so that I help you get an ID, and you will give me 150 Deutschmarks so that I can help you purchase your apartment. My son-in-law gave this money to him in the car immediately. He gave him another 50 and another 150, so all together 200 Deutschmarks more. At the end, he was also supposed to give me a stamp finalising the contract through which the apartment would become my private property, but he got sick. And so on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, we had to come every day from Osijek, but he was at the hospital. However, on Wednesday, Damir Ibralic was brought in, who was supposed to take his place, and the other two that had always been there together with Mile were also present, and they asked, "Did you make arrangements with Mile?" My son-in-law said, "Yes , we did, and we paid for everything." And then he said, "Well, you have to pay another hundred Deutschmarks for Damir. Please come back in half an hour. The contract will be stamped."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after all of these bribes, did you get your contract and your apartment back?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After he put the stamp on my contract, I went across the street to the company where I used to work at, and that's where I got a receipt with which I could pay for my apartment at the bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you got your apartment back and you noticed that it was damaged, things were destroyed, things were taken. Did you give anyone permission, back in 1993, 1992 -- actually, 1993, to use your apartment or to take any of your things, any of your property?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never gave anyone permission. The apartment was simply taken away from me. And I have already told you what happened with the sewing machine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Krgovic. Cross-examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I start with my question, can you tell me, are you feeling all right? Do you need a rest?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm feeling quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. I will be asking you some questions regarding the answers you gave to the Prosecutor today. My questions will be formulated in such a way as to allow you to answer with a "yes," "no," or "I don't know," and if you want to clarify anything, my colleague from the Prosecution can give you time for that in his re-examination. Also, I wish to say that since we share a language in common and all this needs to be interpreted, please make a pause, a brief pause, before you start answering, to avoid confusion and problems for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, at the beginning of your testimony, you mentioned that you were called names, and we are now talking about April 1992. You said that they called you Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I think it might be useful in terms of your introduction if you let the witness know the name of your client. You haven't said who you're acting as counsel for in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Drljacic, I am asking these questions on behalf of Miroslav Tadic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to my question. You said that they called you Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Please allow me. They called us Ustashas because Muslims --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, ma'am. We'll come back to this later. That's precisely my next question, by the way. But please be patient and let's try to stick to the point. You found that derogatory because in the Second World War, if I understood you correctly, some Muslims, and a great number of Croats, were members of the Ustasha movement, whose units committed war crimes during the Second World War; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a single Muslim in Samac who had been an Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you found this name derogatory because of this criminal reputation of Ustasha units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taking out their anger on us. They were not calling us Ustashas because we were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking whether this was insulting to you because they were associating you with the Ustasha movement.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those people were evil, and if you are an honest and decent person, you don't like to be called that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you also mentioned in your testimony you were 9 in 1941.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Jews who were sweeping streets and who suddenly disappeared.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those Jews, were they killed in Samac by those Ustashas who actually took them away to camps and killed them there?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them exactly. I don't know who took them away or where, and whether they were killed. They just vanished without a trace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, I think we are getting into an area which is not relevant for this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, when she was talking about white armbands, said that she associated them with the fate of the Jews in the Second World War, and that is what I wanted to clarify, whether she found the name "Ustasha" derogatory because she knows that those Jews, during the war, were taken with Serbs, together with Serbs to Jasenovac and killed there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not responsible for their past, and I don't want to go back to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness, you should wait for questions from counsel and then answer them. When counsel is addressing the Bench, you don't have to intervene. You are always to answer questions when counsel asks you, all right? You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am going to abandon this subject and move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you referred in your testimony to the fact that in April 1992 the citizens of Bosanski Samac received bread and milk as aid, and if I understood correctly, this bread and milk was distributed to members of all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including you?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this last?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to tender a document which has already been disclosed to the Office of the Prosecutor. It is a list of persons receiving humanitarian aid, drafted by the office of the Red Cross of Bosanski Samac. The ERN number begins with 4806, and the last ERN number is 4814. I also have an authorised English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could counsel read the full ERN number so we can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 0004806 is the first page, and the last page is 0004814. [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one clarification. On the authorised translation we have the organisation identified who drafted the document, and the first and the last name of the person on the last page. That's how we got this translation from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objections to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. You wait for counsel to ask you questions. If there is anything that you want to explain, the Prosecution will deal with that. So just wait for questions from counsel. Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Can we get a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The English translation is D42/3, and the B/C/S is D42/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you have seen this document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, and I protest against it. It says here Republika Srpska, an entity which was totally unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, please.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was no Republika Srpska. Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you wait for questions? Those matters as to what entity or what country, all these things took place in will be dealt with by the Prosecution. So just wait for questions from counsel and answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, please. It is precisely for this reason that I highlighted certain sections. Would you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the left corner it says: Republika Srpska. CPB Samac, Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I told you it said Samac municipality Red Cross, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the heading, it says: List of persons receiving humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was this list drafted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, ma'am. Answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, I think we shall move faster, because we've got the official translation. We all know what the title says. So just ask questions about whatever, but not ask the witness to read anything, because the translation is already here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, have you looked through this list?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your name on the list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you direct her to the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 175. Number 175, page 2.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see my name. I see Drljacic -- oh, my God.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 2, ma'am. You are looking at page 3.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found Bahra Drljacic. Bahra Drljacic was married into Serbia before the war, perhaps 12 years before the war, and she is a citizen of Serbia. She wasn't living in Samac. Then Safet Drljacic died in 1991. He is my brother. Fadila could not be located in Republika Srpska because she was exchanged in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, can I please ask you to turn to page 2, number 175, the right upper corner.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see yourself under number 175?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my name, but I never lived in Republika Srpska before. I left in 1993, on the 24th of December, and Republika Srpska did not exist then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you receive bread and milk in April 1992 from the office of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, yes, but never in Republika Srpska, where I never lived, until now, when I'm going to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, in April 1992, did you receive bread and milk from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said I did, and when we were waiting in line, there is a recording of that. There is footage of that, where you can see that we were standing in the queue wearing those white armbands. The footage was made by Cvijan Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you looked through this list, and you see that Muslims, Croats, and Serbs are equally represented, as far as you can judge by the names?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. We are talking about year 1992, and this list is from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I too am talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have nothing more to discuss, because this list originates from Republika Srpska, which came into power in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you see on this list a number of Muslims, that is, people whom you used to know in 1992 in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen everything, but I don't want to discuss this list any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have seen a great number of Muslims on the list?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise this list. It could not have been true in 1992, because my sister Bahra wasn't there at the time, and she is still in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is somebody's invention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness, you've been told by the Bench that you don't have to discuss anything else other than the questions that counsel puts to you. That way we shall move much faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Counsel, before you move on with the next question, there's no indication of a date on this list, unless I'm missing something somewhere. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the time frame of the drafting of this document, we will present evidence in the Defence case. We will prove in which period it was developed and bring witnesses who worked at the time at the Red Cross office in Bosanski Samac. This document in fact originates from the Red Cross of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Drljacic, in your testimony, you also said at one point that after a while, supply with staples was normalised and shops started to work again.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. There was only one grocery store where we could buy bread. All the other shops were empty and closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said, in response to a question by the Prosecutor, that the butcher's shop was open and that you could buy meat.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was privately owned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the marketplace was also open and you could buy freely everything that was available and displayed?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That much is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that respect, all citizens were equal. Those who could afford it could buy anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with that proviso, if you could afford it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about flour? Did you get it also from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We bought flour. It cost 12 Deutschmark per one sack of 25 kilos and only those people who had the money could buy it, because people hadn't stocked up, because nobody expected this war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you mentioned also that you had heard from your neighbours about many Muslims and Croats who received flour, edible oil, and some other foodstuffs from the Red Cross, and when you went to some office to get the same, you were not able to.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was Stari hotel location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell me, please: Did you get registered anywhere before you went to the local commune or to the Red Cross office to get your ration of flour, milk and other things? Did you get registered anywhere as somebody who was entitled to humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know you could do that. Who could possibly know? At that place where the distribution was effected, you had to sign up for the things you got.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to tender another document, also drafted by the Red Cross of Bosanski Samac, the social Security Service, titled "Criteria for the distribution of basic necessities to the needy." It is dated 25 June 1992. And I also have an official, authorised translation. The number -- [Previous translation continues] [In English] ...004873. [Interpretation] Can we please get a number for this document, unless there are objections from the side of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D43/3 and D43/3 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, have you looked at this document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. I don't know what you want to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, ma'am: You didn't register anywhere at the local commune or at the Red Cross office to apply for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't register or apply because I didn't know. If I had known about this, I would have thought that, as somebody aged over 60, I was entitled to it. I think you could do this at a later stage, after receiving the aid. If you had -- took the time to post other notices and proclamations, you could as well have posted this one on our entrance door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, were you entitled to receive a pension in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, and the last pension that my brother and I received were not enough, taken together, to buy an egg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I understand it that you received a pension in Bosanski Samac in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know under what criteria, but my brother's and my pension taken together at the time were enough to buy only one egg at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the bottom of this paper and see who is signed.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velimir Maslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coordinator of Red Cross affairs and social services?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the gentleman whom I approached. That is my next-door neighbour, whom I approached for advice whether to ask to be exchanged or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't approach him for advice as to whether you are entitled to apply for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him at all, and I never went to the municipality until that time. I didn't even know that he was working there. And when I saw him, I approached him, as a neighbour. But when the war began, he stopped being my neighbour. He no longer lived at his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've finished with this document. Your Honours, I would now like to tender another document, if we have enough time, that is. We have a couple of minutes left, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document - again from the Red Cross, dated 22nd May 1992, titled "List of persons receiving bread and milk from the Red Cross in the fourth quarter." We also have an authorised translation for the Office of the Prosecutor. [In English] 004822 and Y0004823. Any objection from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have our break and then the Prosecution can indicate whether or not they object to the document. We shall have our break and continue the proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, you continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the number for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D44/3 and D44/3 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you please take a look at this document. In May of 1992, were any of these people on this list living in Samac, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if Hajro had already died, Hajro Vukovic. I'm very glad that I got this list, if this list corresponds to the date. I am glad because, as far as you know, the city of Samac had a majority of Muslims. So what happened to all those Muslims that are not on the list and did not have the right to receive food?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you look at this list, half of the names are Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was asking you: How many Muslims lived in the fourth quarter who did not have the right to get this humanitarian aid that we were supposed to receive? This must have been a donation of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Drljacic, do not ask questions to counsel. He is not a witness. So just answer his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, so we can conclude that of the people on this list who were receiving humanitarian aid, the majority were Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but there were 50 more --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would please like you to just keep to my questions. The majority are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but a small percentage of the people living there, the Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my questions only with yes or no. And in May of 1992 they lived in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so. I don't know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender another document. This is a document also belonging to the Red Cross, dated 18th of September, 1992. This is also a list of the Red Cross in Bosanski Samac. It's a list of people that are receiving bread and milk for free in August of 1992. We also have an official translation of this document. I would like the usher to assist me in handing these out. This document has also been given to the Prosecution. I gave the ERN number to the Prosecution a couple of minutes ago as well. [In English] Any objection from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D45/3 and D45/3 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you take a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There's no date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the letterhead. The date is 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing it says is 1992. There is no date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last part of the letterhead. On the first page.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you mean below. Okay. So what next?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you know any of these people? You said while you were answering the questions of the Prosecutor that you know everybody in Bosanski Samac. Do you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me take a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, number 77?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 71, interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Semsa Memsic. Do you know her?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could remind you that she was the mother of Buca Memsic. He was a leader of the SDA and one of the members of the armed units of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know her by this last name or first name. I think I know all the Mesics. I don't know this name, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She worked in Borovo as a shop assistant. Oh, I apologise. Semsa. Okay. So what next?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she live in Samac at this time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August, I'm not sure. I think she left. I don't think she was exchanged, but I think she left. I don't know when, however. I wouldn't be able to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this list, ma'am, there's also a lot of Muslims and Croats, less so than on the first list, but still a large number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether these people lived in Samac at the time or not. How could I know this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is a lot of Muslims on this list, and Croats. Their names are on this list.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 43, Hasan Velic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the father of Dragan Delic, who was arrested and testified in front of this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but who can claim that he got what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please just answer my questions. I think this would be better also because of your health, otherwise we might stay here until midnight. Please, tell me: Was he in Samac at that moment, in August? Did you see him around town?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only that he was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August of 1998 - I apologise, of 1992 - what were the conditions -- in Samac when it comes to buying basic foodstuffs or electricity, was much worse than in April for all citizens of Samac. I'm talking generally speaking. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We had no electricity, no water. Many of us didn't have money to buy food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the following: You were receiving pensions regularly all the time that you were in Samac, although they might have been very small?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did receive them, but that doesn't mean that we could live from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the pensions were received by everybody: Muslims, Croats, and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your neighbours - Muslims, Croats, and your brother and your relatives that you knew - were receiving pensions?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was receiving mine as well, but there was no way I could live off of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the inflation, I assume, which was enormous; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, while you testified, you mentioned refugees. You mentioned that refugees showed up in Bosanski Samac, even that some Serb refugees, if I understood correctly, were placed in your brother's establishment after this establishment, this shop was closed?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Serb refugees in Samac while I was there, until December of 1993. I don't know of any refugees. I know that one group came from Bijeljina. They protested for two days in the school -- actually, in front of the school, in the playground area. They said that there was 200 of them. They came from Bijeljina and they protested because they did not get what they were promised. And then they came to Samac. They heard that there were empty houses there. One family that I saw move into a destroyed house, this house belonged to Ante Saric, and there was an old lady there, much -- I think she was older than I am now. They all protested. And this grandmother told us that they were told to go to Prud and that all the houses there were empty, that there was a lot of land there. And they said if we had wanted to work on the land, then we wouldn't come here, and that's not what we wanted. This was a Serb refugee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I was talking generally speaking. So there were refugees from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know of this first instance. This was already happening in 1993, in the summer of 1993. I don't know exactly which month it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender a document of the Red Cross in Samac, dated the 3rd of November, 1992. This is a letter of the president of the Red Cross in Bosanski Samac, Milorad Mihajlovic, to the UNHCR. And this letter is about the numbers and also the housing of refugees. The Prosecution has seen -- we have disclosed this document to the Prosecution. We also have an official translation of this document. [In English] Any objection from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D46/3 and D46/3 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can I say about it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Milorad Mihajlovic, the president of the Red Cross before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read this fact that was given to the UNHCR which says that there's 5.806 refugees, of which 3.480 are women?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're still claiming that in November of 1992 there were no refugees in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that while I was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at this, this document says municipality of Bosanski Samac, which is the town of Bosanski Samac and all of the surrounding villages. She has been talking about the town of Bosanski Samac, the town itself, where she lives, as opposed to the municipality, which is kind of like a county or a municipal area, which takes in a lot of villages, hamlets, towns. We're talking two different matters here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I please respond to this? I asked this question -- I know that it's about the municipality, but while the witness testified to the Prosecution, she was talking about the conditions in the municipality. She was talking about Zasavica and other municipalities. So I assume that she knew about these issues, about the whole municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't -- I can't really know, because we had no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned five or six families in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked about the town of Bosanski Samac, and that's what we were referring to. When we talked about Zasavica and outside areas, we would refer to them by name. That's why I questioned about Zasavica. It's the question I thought was taken out of context, Your Honour, and it was an improper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I think you understand what the Prosecution is talking about. Either you are talking about refugees from the town itself or the municipality, which includes other villages around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, let me ask you the following: In the town of Bosanski Samac, from what you say, there were no refugees.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in such high numbers that you would notice it on the streets, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ma'am, let me ask you the following: We're talking about April of 1992. Did you notice in your neighbourhood any refugees, or in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in April of 1992, December 1993, there had been a large number of Muslim refugees that came from Zvornik, Bijeljina, and other war torn areas and they came to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender a document. This is a document of the Red Cross of Bosanski Samac. The document is dated 17th of July, 1992 and it is about receipt of the Red Cross -- certificate, actually, of the Red Cross, with which a certain person is given a refugee status. This document has been disclosed to the Prosecution, and we also have an official translation which we would like to show to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you take a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not done reading it yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have no objection. In fact, Your Honour, to save time, I have no objection to his other documents, the other documents he has too. You don't even have to stop and ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D47/3 and D47/3 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you take a look at this document, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. So what do you want from me now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of this person, Nedzija Halilovic, son of Nedzad, is this a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this man or woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether this was a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any old name could have been written here. I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was not if you knew him. My question was if this was a Muslim name that was on this document, a name belonging to a man of Muslim or Bosniak ethnicity, if that's how you would like me to call it.

utterances.speaker: HAJRIJA DRLJACIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it's a Muslim name, but what do you want from me about this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I wanted is your answer, which you just gave me, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have another document that is dated 9 of July 1972 [As interpreted]. This is also a certificate of the Red Cross in Bosanski Samac, with which a refugee is given that status. This document, just like the previous one, has been disclosed to the Prosecution, and we also have the English translation. I would like the usher to take the document from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D48/3 and D48/3 ter, Your Honours.
